content: 1. The presence or absence of personal flotation devices (PFDs) was documented in reports investigating boating-related drowning incidents. 2. Among the 137 drowning cases analyzed, 115 (84%) occurred in males. 3. Black and white individuals died in nearly equal numbers, with 68 (50%) and 67 (49%) deaths, respectively. However, the drowning rate among Black individuals was more than twice that of white individuals, at 4.8 per 100,000 compared to 2.3 per 100,000. 4. The median age of individuals who drowned was 32 years, with a range spanning from 10 months to 94 years. 5. The highest drowning rate was observed in individuals aged 25–35 years, at 3.8 per 100,000. 6. Children under the age of 4 accounted for 10% of the total deaths and had the second-highest drowning rate, at 3.5 per 100,000. 7. Among cases where the manner of death could be determined, 122 (95%) were classified as accidental (unintentional), while 7 (5%) were classified as suicides. 8. Twelve (9%) of the drowning deaths were work-related. 9. Of the 114 deaths with coroner or Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) records, 83 (73%) occurred in natural bodies of water (e.g., lakes, bayous, rivers, and the Gulf of Mexico), 19 (17%) in swimming pools, and 7 (6%) in bathtubs or hot tubs. 10. Four deaths were classified as occurring in other settings, and in one case, the setting was unknown. 11. Alcohol testing was conducted in 72 (76%) of the 94 decedents aged over 13 years. Among these, 43 (60%) showed evidence of alcohol and/or illicit drug use. 12. Thirteen (30%) of the decedents tested positive for both alcohol and illicit drugs, 28 (67%) tested positive for alcohol alone, and 1 (2%) tested positive for illicit drugs alone. 13. Among the 19 deaths that occurred in swimming pools, 11 (58%) involved children under the age of 14. 14. Children under the age of 4 had the highest drowning rate in swimming pools, at 1.3 per 100,000. 15. The presence or absence of fencing was noted in 8 (42%) of the swimming pool-related deaths. Six pools had fencing, while two did not. 16. Coroner and LDWF reports indicated that 35 (31%) of the 114 deaths occurred during boating-related activities. Of these, 11 (31%) involved a fall from the boat, 7 (20%) occurred when the boat capsized, and 6 (17%) involved a collision. 17. Five (14%) individuals who drowned had voluntarily entered the water, while 6 (17%) entered the water for unknown reasons. 18. PFD use was recorded in 22 (63%) of the boating-related drowning cases. However, only one individual was wearing a PFD, and it was unfastened. 19. Among individuals aged over 13 years, 34 boating-related drownings occurred, and 13 (48%) tested positive for alcohol or illicit drugs. 20. The findings in this report emphasize the importance of drowning prevention strategies, including reducing alcohol and illicit drug use among both boating passengers and operators, promoting the proper use of PFDs across all age groups, and ensuring adequate supervision and fencing around swimming pools. 21. For a pool fence to effectively prevent drowning, it must completely enclose the pool, be at least 4 feet high, have vertical openings less than 4 inches wide, and include a functional self-latching gate. 22. Prevention efforts should be culturally tailored to address the highest-risk populations. 23. Boating safety improved in the United States during the 1990s, with a 32% decline in the boating fatality rate from 1990 to 1999, despite a 15% increase in registered boats. However, boating-related deaths continue to occur, with 734 fatalities reported in 1999. 24. Capsizing and falling overboard account for more than half of all recreational boating deaths annually. 25. Boaters should consistently wear personal flotation devices (PFDs) and avoid consuming alcohol while boating, as alcohol impairs judgment, vision, balance, and coordination. 26. Approximately one-third of all deaths caused by boating collisions involve alcohol use. 27. Boaters should also be aware of the risk of carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, which can result from sources such as onboard motor generators, gasoline-powered engines, or improper cabin ventilation. 28. 29. Boaters should familiarize themselves with potential hazards and regulations associated with operating a boat. 30. Boating education courses teach the regulatory and statutory rules for safely operating and navigating recreational boats. 31. The U.S. Coast Guard Auxiliary and U.S. Power Squadron offer the Vessel Safety Check (VSC) program, which promotes boating safety by inspecting safety equipment and providing information on equipment use, safety procedures, and applicable regulations. 32. Recommendations for managing fecal accidents in disinfected recreational water venues include removing as much fecal material as possible using a net or scoop, disinfecting the equipment, and raising the free available chlorine concentration to 2 mg/L with a pH of 7.2–7.5. 33. Proper handling of chlorinated disinfectants is essential to prevent injury, and occupational safety and health requirements should be followed.
